utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We welcome you back after your busy endeavours during the break. Now, before we formally turn to Mr. Mansfield, are there any matters still unresolved that have arisen during the break concerning the provision of the Defence materials as required by the Rules before the commencement of the Defence cases? Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. There are two minor matters that relate both to the Defence of Mr. Musliu. First, we had been promised more complete 65 ter summaries of the 92 bis statements some time ago. It's my understanding that we received them just minutes before coming into court today, so I have not had an opportunity to look at them. But assuming that they are complete then that issue will have been resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have you had the statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, and that was going to be my next point. I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Because if you had the statements, I would have thought the summaries were not very material.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, that's correct, Your Honour. We wouldn't have pressed for the summaries if we had the statements. And of course the -- we would like to be able to agree on 92 bis statements, but we can't do that unless we see the statements. It also impairs our preparation to meet the Defence case if we don't have the statements. It's my -- just looking at the brief summaries that I have seen, I don't think that it's likely we will be able to agree on all the statements with respect to 92 bis. They don't appear to satisfy the requirements of the Rule just from the summary. So I would just ask that the statements be provided to the Prosecution as soon as possible so that either they can be agreed upon, redactions can be made, or they can be litigated if that's necessary. Or the witness can be brought to testify live if that's -- if that's also a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This affects only -- sorry. This affects only the Rule 92 bis witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that's correct. I don't -- unfortunately, there is not yet, I think, a rule requiring the Defence to provide statements of other witnesses who are going to testify viva voce. If there were such a rule, would I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were you anticipating by the word "yet" that that will change?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Actually, think there is some discussion about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is discussion, yes. Unfortunately, I'm a member of the Rules Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I won't press for the Court's view on that matter. In any event, I think it's clear how the Rule stands now, and while we would appreciate having the prior statements of the witnesses, I don't think that we have a legal basis to press for them to be provided to us. So, yes, it does just relate to the 92 bis statements, where of course we have to have the statements in order to take a position on them. And that -- while I said at the beginning that these matters relate only to Mr. Musliu, that -- that point with respect to the 92 bis statements actually relates to, I believe, at least to the Limaj Defence because I think they have some proposed 92 bis statements. I don't believe that Mr. Bala has any proposed 92 bis statements, but I may be mistaken about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, before you sit, Mr. Whiting, where have you reached with exhibit lists and copies of exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that was the next point. The -- with respect to the Defence for Mr. Bala and Mr. Limaj, we have received both exhibit lists and copies of exhibits within the last few days. With respect to Mr. Musliu, we have received neither an exhibit list nor any exhibits, and I would ask again that those be provided to us or that it be put on the record that there are no exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And what about expert witnesses' reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We have received one expert witness report, and we have discussed the matter with the Defence and it is agreed that he will testify next week. That's the second witness. There has been indication of additional experts through the -- through the 65 ter summaries, but we have not yet received those reports, and I would urge those reports to be provided as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Any other issue that you anticipated raising?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It might be convenient to start with Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, if that start needs to begin with an apology, it is made. Mr. Whiting is quite right. The 65 ter summaries in their fuller version were served today. May I ask that we be indulged to this extent regarding 92 bis, that we will meet with Mr. Whiting and agree what I hope he will find to be an appropriate timetable. The statements are in unsigned form in their present format. That is being dealt with literally as I speak, and that of course involves them going either physically or electronically to Kosova and being seen, checked, signed, and returned. And that is an ongoing process, as I say, as I understand it as I address you this afternoon. As far as exhibits are concerned, with the possible, I underline the word possible, exception of a video or two, we are not relying upon any exhibits, as I presently understand the case for Mr. Musliu, beyond those, of course, which have already been put in and exhibited as part of the Prosecutor's case. There was a significant difficulty in viewing videos at the UNDU during the course of Your Honours' break in the case. That has been resolved. We, again with your permission and leave, will liaise directly with Mr. Whiting and his team over that matter in the hope again that there will be no difficulty in due course in presenting that material should we choose to do so to the Court as part of Mr. Musliu's case, which on current predictions is or could be at least a month away. But, Your Honour, that is not being taken as any excuse nor justification for any further delays as far as all of these aspects are concerned. I can assure you that we have not been idle over the break. There have, as you can appreciate, been difficulties with various members of the team physically located in different countries, not least Mr. Musliu being here. And I hope, therefore, that the Court will -- Tribunal will have some understanding and appreciation of the difficulties that such problems give rise to. And again, as I began, if any inconvenience has been caused, I apologise. But more than that, one is anxious of course that we comply with the Rules, and I am making it my business to ensure we do as quickly and as completely as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Topolski. I can pass Mr. Guy-Smith by. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon. The position I think as far as we're concerned is virtually complete. So far as statements, 92 bis statements are concerned, the Prosecution do have our summaries. I think they are uncontroversial. They concern three witnesses who relate the extent to which Fatmir Limaj appeared on television at various times, so I don't think there's going to be an issue about any of those. But we don't have their statements yet, and as soon as we do, we'll ensure that the Prosecution have them, but we've asked for them. But that's the content. So far as experts are concerned, if I may pass to that topic, clearly we've obviously given a list of witnesses, and I'm grateful for the agreement over Mr. Churcher who can really only come next week, and we've agreed a timing for that. The other expert, and I'll mention it now, as far as our list is concerned, is number 16 on the list, Professor Wagenaar, and his name may already be known to you from other cases. He deals with the processes of identification generally and also in this case. We do have a draft report. We are awaiting a joint conference with him. He affects actually all three cases, and the intention at the moment, at least provisional intention since it's plain we're not going to be able to serve in time for him to be called as part of my case, but hopefully it will all be sorted such that Mr. Topolski, who comes last and has already indicated at least a month between now and the start of his case, that the professor might be called as part of his case, towards the end of his case. So we hope to rectify that situation. I'm sorry it's taken a bit longer to solidify what is being said there. It's relatively detailed. But that's the position. So may I say at once I don't think Mr. Whiting need at the moment concern himself that it will -- he will come as part of Mr. Limaj's case. I can undertake that he won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for the moment. Mr. Topolski, I'm sorry, experts other than Professor Wagenaar?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a possibility of only one other, and that is a psychologist who has been in to see Mr. Musliu once in the earlier part of trial. He is someone, again, we are meeting Mr. Powles and I and others in my team are meeting with next week, I hope, to discuss a further consultation. And I will therefore know and again personally undertake to advise Mr. Whiting whether there is any serious prospect of any evidence from that quarter being deployed, again only as part of Mr. Musliu's case. I recognise that with such a -- such a category of evidence, I should say, early service of any report upon which one relies is doubly important upon the basis of another expert being potentially deployed to counter him or her. Your Honour, again there have been difficulties. Unless I'm asked to, I won't elaborate upon them now, but that is the only other expert area that could conceivably touch upon the case of Mr. Musliu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith, was there any prospect or is there any prospect of expert evidence from the point of view of your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There is the possibility of one expert who is presently in consultation that deals directly with an issue that comes before this court on a number of occasions with regard to Mr. Bala and specifically obviously deals with his physical condition. Whether or not the specific conclusions to be drawn will go directly to some of the issues that exist actually within the case or not is still a matter which is open and we should have an answer in the relatively near future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting, it is suggested by Mr. Topolski that there might be discussions concerning the Rule 92 bis summaries and statements and the exhibit copies. Is that something that you would see as adequate for the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, with respect to exhibit and 92 bis statements, certainly. I think that that's perfectly satisfactory and I don't anticipate any difficulty. I would make two points, however. The first is with respect to exhibits. I think that -- I've heard about the video, the potential video that the Musliu Defence might rely on already. I heard about it a couple of weeks ago from -- I think from Mr. Powles. And I would just -- I would just submit that the Defence should -- should, like the Prosecution, err on the side of disclosure. When they're unsure if an exhibit is going to be used it shouldn't be at the last minute when there is absolute certainty that the exhibit is disclosed. I would ask that it be -- if they're considering it that it be disclosed as soon as possible. The second point, and this is to -- with respect to experts and it's to follow on from what Mr. Topolski said about the need for early disclosure of expert reports. Rule 94 bis, of course, talks about -- has a 30-day requirement where the opposing side has 30 days to respond to an expert report about whether it will accept the report or require cross-examination. I don't think that that 30-day requirement should be interpreted as being the minimum that -- the time of disclosure. That is, it's not the same as, well, we can -- we can disclose the report and then call the witness within 30 days. With experts, often more time is required to -- to digest the report, consult with other experts, to fully prepare to have the expert come and testify and possibly get an expert to consult for the Prosecution. With the Churcher report, we are having the witness come almost to the day 30 days after the report was provided to us, and in that case it's been difficult to prepare fully for it but it's been possible in part because he is an expert in a sense responding to our expert. But with the Wagenaar report, I'm a little concerned about having only 30 days to prepare to respond to that report, and so the time is running. The Defence has told me they anticipate the case to be seven weeks long now. If we don't get the report soon, we're not going to have enough time to prepare to respond to it, especially as -- as it apparently deals with all three accused. So I don't know. Perhaps it would be visible if possible to set a date when the report can be provided to us, especially since it's now already -- there's a draft report. Maybe by the beginning of next week it could be provided to us, end of this week, I don't know. But I would press very strongly for that report to be provided to us as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I ask Mr. Mansfield how soon it would be practical to give, at least to draft in adequate shape to Mr. Whiting of the expert reports that are being considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. One of the problems is arranging a joint conference but that we're arranging at the moment. I will ask for 14 -- we will serve within 14 days of today but that may be perhaps to Mr. Whiting too long, but I would ask for that, because we're also dealing with Mr. Churcher who is arriving here next Monday and we're trying to correlate the two. The other thing that obviously must be known to the Prosecution already is that this particular witness, Professor Wagenaar, has already given evidence in other cases and so the gist of what he's saying is in fact clearly set out in the Tadic case, and we have a transcript of that, and we can in fact provide that if they don't already have it. But I understand obviously what Mr. Whiting is really saying: We need to know what he's saying in this case in relation to all three defendants. And so I ask for a little longer than next Monday because I think we may not have had the final conference, joint conference, with him before that date. That's the only thing. So if we could have a little leeway on that. Certainly I would undertake within 14, did you if you feel that that's too much time, then I don't know, within ten days certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I definitely concur in that request. I believe that we will be able to set up the joint conference in short order, and once that's done, we'll get it to Mr. Whiting and the others as quickly as possible and certainly within the 14-day request that's been made by Mr. Mansfield. And obviously if they need any more time or if there are any difficulties, we certainly wouldn't wish to put him too far ahead of the game with regard to testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Anything to add, Mr. Topolski?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would indicate that service of that report should be effected by midday of Thursday of next week, which a little less than Mr. Mansfield had hoped for but should be adequate. Now, if there are other expert reports, clearly the same concern of Mr. Whiting would apply to those, and we would hope that there would be an early advice to Mr. Whiting of any decision to call an expert, and if one is under serious consideration that they might be made available at the earliest opportunity, even a draft report, so that we don't run into impractical problems which necessitate delay or put everybody under unnecessary pressure. As for the other matters yet to be dealt with, the Chamber at the moment is prepared to accept the suggestion of Mr. Topolski that counsel might confer to resolve those. And that leaves the Chamber with just one concern of its own. That is when the estimates given so confidently of the length of the Defence case just before we broke are still maintained. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Overall, yes. As far as my case is concerned, or that of Mr. Limaj's is concerned, because we were unaware that there were going to be two days lost this week, the three-week, I'm afraid, estimate trickles into the fourth for obvious reasons. But that's the only amendment. Otherwise, we are relatively confident we're going to meet those deadlines. Overall, I think, in fact the same position, but I don't want to speak for others, but I think we are hoping to meet the deadline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your list of witnesses would seem to suggest otherwise at first glance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, it's the first blush, I'm afraid. The second blush means that -- we have indicated this to Mr. Whiting. In fact, this very evening we're going to decide whether we really do need -- we were accepting the approach that Mr. Whiting offered earlier that we should err on the side of disclosure. So that is what we've done. That's the raft of witnesses. But we have made it very clear and I certainly personally left a message for him that the end of the day, and I say now it's unlikely we'll call all of them because some of them are repetitious and we're certainly not wishing to make the point more than once unless it's really necessary. So there will be less witnesses, and some of them are very short. The longer ones are at the front; that's this week, next week and possibly the beginning of the following week. But after that they should be relatively quick. So that's how we worked it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any other revision of estimates at the moment? Not, I see, from Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: After I'd left, Mr. Powles told you two to three weeks, I think for Mr. Musliu's case, and I agree with that estimate. If I were to introduce a cloud onto the horizon, I would suppose one would have to say subject to agreement regarding the 92 bis witnesses. But I personally can see no difficulty there. And the estimate given for the Musliu case of two to three weeks was one given with Mr. Powles and I having discussed that as a prospect in any event. And therefore the short answer to Your Honour's question is no revision, as I speak, and indeed I would anticipate from the way certain matters are developing be in a similar situation as to Mr. Mansfield and not necessarily calling all of those as live witness who is currently appear on our list to be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Topolski. It will be obviously -- obvious to you and Mr. Mansfield that at present the Prosecution are no doubt preparing for the full list. If you're going to remove a significant number of names, their task becomes more practical and manageable, as does the Chamber's if the list can be revised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I may say so, I think I speak on behalf of the whole of the Defence bar. We, too, prepared for all of the Prosecution's witnesses to be called as part of their case and was pleased when Mr. Whiting was able regularly to tell us that he was not intending to call one or other or indeed several, in fact, I can say many. And so we will reciprocate as best we can. It's been a case, if I may say so, marked for its level of cooperation, and I see no reason why that should not continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber is grateful for the efforts that have been made by counsel so far and looks forward to a continuation of that mood. Mr. Mansfield, that brings us to the commencement of your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. May I call Fatmir Limaj, please, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. straightaway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If Mr. Limaj would come to the witness position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And while he's doing that, may I just check with Your Honours there is an exhibit list you should have which indicates maps. They're mainly maps, and there is a DVD which may -- we may reach today, we may not. The maps are on your own DVDs. We haven't got hard copies yet. They may be available tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Limaj, if you would good enough to take the affirmation that is on the card handed to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, can I just test that the acoustics are all right and you can hear adequately. Is that comfortable now?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Yeah, it's okay now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: You pointed out I think only one microphone is on. Perhaps two should be, I'm not sure. There are two in front and I think there's another. Yes. Thank you. Mr. Limaj, I'm going to ask you questions in a chronological order, because it's easier for you and it's easier for everyone else to follow what you have to say. And so that it's clear to you and also to others, most of today will be concerned with background matters, but we may reach obviously the crucial period in 1998 later on today. But mostly background. So I'm going to start with the obvious question. It's going to be the only one that I'm going to lead you on. Is it right that you were born on the 4th of February, 1971?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: I was born in Banje, previously part of Suva Reka commune. And then in 1986 it became part of Malisheve municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Just for these purposes but we'll have to come back to it a number of times, we'll try out the exhibits. The first map that I want to use in relation to obviously your home and your birthplace and other matters is map number 1, which is to your left-hand side on the board.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And Your Honours have it on a CD as well if you wish to follow. But the village, your birthplace and other matters is map number 1, which is to your left-hand side on the board. And Your Honours have it on a CD as well if you wish to follow. But the village, your birthplace is marked very clearly on the map on the board. If Your Honours also wish to see exactly where it is, that is Banje his birthplace, it is also marked on Prosecution Exhibit 1, map 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: But could you -- I don't know whether you can reach it from where you're sitting, but could you please point out where your birthplace is on the map on the left-hand side which is a large-scale map.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Banje is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, it might be acceptable because in the longer run I'm going to ask if this map -- you're going to have a mark a number of places will become relevant. If you circled a number of those key areas. Is there a marker, a pen you could use. If you could kindly stand up and mark it so that we can it see when this becomes an exhibit. Just circle Banje.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the first question about your birthplace is how big a place is it in terms of numbers? Certainly at the time -- you wouldn't have known at the time you were born obviously how many were there, but roughly speaking over the intervening years, what is the population of that village?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: If we are talking about the present, it must have about 3.000 inhabitants. I want to tell you however, that Banje is a very beautiful and tourist village, and unlike other villages of Malisheve municipality, it is one of the most developed village. And given that, there are often people visiting the village and settling there from other regions. But generally, I would say -- give an estimate of 3.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you a little bit about your parents and your family. First of all, how many brothers or sisters do you have?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: As I have said in my opening statement, we are three brothers and three sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And so far as your parents are concerned, were either of your parents -- have they been working throughout this period we're dealing with, that is 1971 onwards? Were they working during this time?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Yes. My dad worked since he was 14, 15 years of age. But he started to have a permanent job first in Sarajevo, if I am not mistaken, in the early 1960s, and he worked until 1982 or 3 when he returned in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And what was the work that he did in Pristina from 1982 or 1983 when he returned there?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: After he returned to Pristina, he had a house, an apartment in Sarajevo given to him from the company he worked for, because at that time it was customary for a company to provide accommodation to its workers. After that, my father was in a position to trade that apartment with another. That person helped him find a job in Pristina. He worked in the Electroeconomy enterprise in Kosova, Banje village. Because there -- it was very difficult then to find a job. He refused to return to Kosova before he was certain to have a proper job, and having a house or an apartment was the condition for him to make the decision to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, a little bit more about yourself in the early years. Where did you attend elementary or primary school?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: I attended my primary school in my hometown, because as I said, my father was in Sarajevo. It was my uncle who took care of us, and we lived together with his family, for him to take care of us kids since my father was in Sarajevo. So I finished my primary in Banje of Malisheve. After completing the primary school in Banje, I went on for two years. I did two years of the high school. The system was such that for two years it was like a preliminary course. Then after that, after two years, you had to make your own decision as to what you wanted to study.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could he please -- ask to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: You're speaking very fast for the interpreters. So if you could just take it more slowly. And may I just, therefore, use this opportunity to go back one phase. At what age would you have finished your primary school?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: I entered primary school at the age of 6, and then I finished it in 1984, 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: That's the primary education. And the secondary school that you began doing the course, where was that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: I started high school immediately, that is in 1984, 1985, I think. 1985, in fact. I went for two years in Banje in Malisheve. It was -- it was a parallel school from the one in Suva Reka called "Jete Ere" [phoen], New Life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And after two years where did you move to?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: After two years I continued my studies in Pristina, in the high school in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And by that time, the time you moved to Pristina, how old were you then?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Sixteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Sixteen. I want to pause for a moment --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Sixteen going to 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. I want to just reflect on the first, therefore, 16 years. Where did you -- in those 16 years, where did you spend most of your time, your youthful time?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: In my native down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And where were all your friends? Were they also in the native town or other towns? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Normally it's not a town. It's like a village. Most of them were friends from that area. Some others came from a larger area. You know, Banje was a kind of local unit comprising three or four neighbouring villages, and all of them had -- all the children of these villages went to the same school in Banje. I mean the high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: During that time - we're dealing with the first 16 years - did you have occasion to go visit relatives or friends in other villages other than Banje and, if so, which villages were they in that period?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Family ties in Kosova are very strong and powerful, so it was common for me to see my extended family, if I might say so, that is my uncles, my aunts on my father's side or on my mother's side, and other in-laws, because ours was a rather large family. So it was customary for us to go and visit our relatives in other villages where they were living. There were occasions when I also visit my friends. I had friends in various villages. So we kept links with one another. Sometimes it happened that we visited our classmates on the occasions of birthdays or other occasions. Apart from that, there were other occasions that we visited one another as part of daily life and work, because they were all surrounding villages very close to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, there is obviously a purpose behind these questions, so I wonder if you'd be kind enough to just return to the map for a moment if the villages are marked. You've indicated there are villages relating to relatives, villages relating to friends. Could you just on that map, you've marked Banje already, if there are other villages on that that you would have gone in these first 16 years, if you could just ring those as well if they're there on that map. It's to your left-hand side on the board.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: If you are kind enough to ask me about the villages where I have relatives? Or you want me to indicate the villages I have travelled to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: We'll deal with the relatives first. So if you could stand up and just ring the ones with relatives in, first of all. This is in the first 16 years. If you could just call the names as you do it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters cannot hear what the witness is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: We'll have to point one of the microphones. Can I just repeat it. I think you said Belanica.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Bellanice is the native village of my mother. It's a village where I used to go very frequently when I was a child with my mother and alone, and I knew it almost as much always I knew Banje. Then there is a village here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Its name, please?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Carralluke, it's called, where my aunt on my father's side lives. Then comes this -- this village here, Kravosari. We used to go there often because my uncle had relatives there. Then Lladrovic village. The aunts of my father lived there. Then Blac. Some distant relatives, but for us it was a common practice to visit even distant relatives on -- in weddings or for funerals. Klecka is the place where my -- the father -- the sister of my father lives, my aunt, that is. I visited regularly. These are some of the villages that I used to go to. There are some others, but they are part of Suhareke municipality. They are not part of this map here. But I can tell you that Suhareke was part of an adjoining municipality. So we had occasion to visit all these villages although we didn't have family links.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, in this period --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I could -- could you point the microphone back towards you. Thank you. Now, in this period I'm going to ask you the direct question here: Did you ever have occasion in these 16 years to go to Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: The village is situated along the road linking Pristina to Malisheve, which at that time was not a municipality but a large commune. So I have travelled along the villages situated along the main road, but I have not stopped there because I didn't have anything to do with then. I just happened to pass by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to move to the next period. You're 16, approximately, and you are finishing your studies, school studies, by going to Pristina. Where did you live in Pristina while you were completing your school studies, first of all?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: As I said earlier, because my father was living in -- he had found an apartment in Pristina, and one of the reasons for that, was to enable us to learn in our mother tongue in the capital of Kosova. While I was in primary school, I used to -- to study in Albanian during the weekends, but -- and I wanted to go to Pristina, but at that time it was difficult to go from one school to another, to transfer to a new school. So after finishing the two years of the high school, I went on to Pristina where I lived in the house of my father, that is, with my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I just want to ask you this: By this age, 16, 17, were you conscious or aware of the political developments taking place in Kosovo, and were you interested in those?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Not at that time, because we were kids, teenagers. We didn't have such interests. However, developments in 1981 had their impact on all, but you might imagine how much can a 15- or a 16-year-old know of what is going on. However, as I said, they had an impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I just want to pause for a moment in relation to 1981. How did you learn about the events of 1981? And perhaps as a first question, what were the events of 1981 to which you are referring?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: In 1981, I was ten years old, and so I heard what other people said, because in my native town it was difficult to know what was going on. And even to hear about what was going on was difficult for us living in the village, because there was a very great censorship. Afterwards, I heard from grown-ups. I saw some of my classmates telling us that his father was in prison or so. The movement from 1981 was a student movement called the Spring of 1981. The demands of that movement were to improve the social life of the Albanians in Kosovo. After that, then they demanded political rights for Kosovo to be recognised, the right as the seventh republic of Yugoslavia. After these demands and some demonstrations staged in the streets, the then forces of Yugoslavia exerted pressure and terror against the demonstrators to disband them and to put down their demands and -- and they imprisoned hundreds of people. Thousands of students were expelled from school. Some were killed. All of these were things which I heard much later, because as I said -- you might imagine that under a communist regime it was very difficult for information to leak. It was very tight censorship. All these things I realised later, 1989, 1990, actually, when I could meet some of the then participants of that movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, coming to that particular moment in time, 1989 -- an important year for other reasons, obviously, but in 1989, 1990, where were you studying at that point?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: In 1989, I began my studies at the Faculty of Law in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: What were you studying?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: I was studying law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Any particular aspect of law were you studying?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Our system, education system, at that time did not include any division. It was a general faculty, the Faculty of Law. It didn't have any particular or specialised branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: You indicated that it was in the later period you learnt about people's testimony as to what had been happening in 1981 and since then. Did you meet any particular people that you recall in this period whilst you were at the university in the Faculty of Law with whom you became particularly friendly?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: As for a person who could have participated in the events then, no, but I have met people who took part in these demonstrations. However, they did not have any particular role in those demonstrations. If you refer to the leaders of those demonstrations, I didn't meet any. I just met with participants. Those who participated in those demonstrations, those who were imprisoned, they had to continue with their studies later, and that's why we studied together later on, and these people became our colleagues even though they were older than us. However, I had the opportunity to meet with family members of those who spent time in prison. In 1989, 1990, information began to circulate in areas regarding the situation and the conditions of the imprisonment of political prisoners. Also, I had the opportunity to listen to some of the interviews with these persons, for example Adem Demaqi. He gave an interview to a Croatian newspaper. So basically these were conversations that students have amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: During your time at university -- you graduated, I think, in 1995, so we're dealing with a four- to five-year period. During that period, did you become politically active yourself?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: I graduated in 1994. In Kosova, from 1987 or 1988, development was rapid. Kosovo entered an entirely new phase. In 1988, in November, this time in Kosovo is known as people's movement. This all popular movement is called such because people demanded amendments to the constitution. The Serbian regime at that time debated the constitutional changes in Yugoslavia at that time, and at that time the system of public debates was implied. These constitutional changes foresaw the changes to the constitution of Kosovo as well. And also, the diminishing of the competence from the Kosovars themselves. So people through these public debates they expressed their views which were that they were against these changes. They were against these constitutional changes. After these public debates the protests took place, public manifestations where citizens, publicly, and coming from all other Kosova, came to Pristina, and they publicly expressed their opposition to the tendencies of changing the constitution and to -- to express their public support for the then leadership of Kosova, which at the time was constantly attacked by the Serbian Communist Party in Belgrade. After these developments of 1988, some of the Kosovar leaders were removed from their positions. The federal government under the Serbian pressure condemned this public manifestation of the Kosovar citizens by accusing the Kosovar leadership as one of the organisers of the pan-popular movement. As a result of this, some of the Kosovar leaders were imprisoned, some were isolated. In a way, this gave a way to the constitutional changes that Serbia introduced in 1989. I would like to say that behind all these developments were the youth of Kosova and the workers, including those who worked in the Kosova mines at that time. After these repressive measures undertaken by the federal government under the Serbian pressure in 1988 and after the arrest of some of the leaders, Kosovar leaders, and saying that Serbia was moving towards its decision and that it's not to change the -- to deprive Kosova from its autonomy. In February of 1989, the method of protest changed and workers went on a hunger strike, and the situation of hunger strike continued until the time when the federal government stopped the anti-constitutional methods that were exercised by the Serb regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. It's a very long answer. The question, in fact, was this: To what extent did you yourself against this background become involved in any political discussions, political movement, political process? We're dealing with 1988, 1989, 1990.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Maybe I was long, but this was an experience that was experienced by all citizens of Kosova, and I was part of this as well as every other citizen of Kosova who is interested in the fate of its own country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: It might be helpful if you could describe - I'm sorry to bring it down to the particular - how these changes affected you on a daily basis, and your fellow students. I mean, what changes were brought about at the university, for example?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Well, everybody felt differently. As young students, we wanted to be part of this, to be in the leadership of these protests in order to defend our autonomy. And we were convinced that we were asking for our own rights, that those measures were anti-constitutional. Shortly, we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wanted to undertake preventive measures that would avoid them depriving us of those little rights that we were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: What were the preventive measures that you had in mind for that period?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: To our opinion was -- a preventive measures was to make it clear to the government that the citizens were not satisfied with the changes, and at that time the only forum to make it clear to the government was through these public manifestations and protests. So this was in order to draw the attention to the federal government who was implementing these changes to the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Did matters improve at the university? Did it get better or worse?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: No. On the contrary. Things turned the way people feared. As I said earlier, our protests were answered with repression. They proclaimed us enemies of Yugoslavia. These are expressions that they constantly used, especially after 1981. I would like to add that over 1 million people participated in these gatherings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, as we progress through the 1990s, 1990, 1991, 1992, 1993, what else was happening with regard to effectively the Serb occupation of Kosovo in those years? Can you just give a description of life in Kosovo for a young man such as yourself.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Maybe it's important to point out that in 1989, Serbia, by implementing measures of pressure and by encircling the Assembly of Kosovo with tanks in order to implement the changes -- to implement the constitutional changes, the situation became worse when we came to the proclamation of the state of emergency declared in Kosova. In 1990, or it was the end of 1989, the new democratic era started and the pluralist system was established. Some efforts were made in Kosova to create new political alternatives. And some political groups were formed which then were transformed into a popular movement. In 1989, the Albanian parliament of Kosova, the legitimate parliament, decided to issue the statement of July the 2nd, known as such all over Kosova, being unable to do it within the premises of parliament because at that time the leadership of the Kosova parliament - the leader was one of Milosevic's trusted men - they declared the statement before the parliament premises in two words and trying to give the gist of it. The statement of July the 2nd declared unlawful what happened in 1989, because they were considered unlawful. That is a decision to deprive Kosova of its autonomy, and that the status of Kosova, it was said, would wait to see how the Yugoslav FEDERATION is going to be reformulated. Because efforts made in various republics at that time demanding constitutional amendments. So they said that Kosova would be willing to participate in a new Yugoslav concoction, having equal status to other republics, but Kosova will not participate if the other republics are not going to participate. This statement is known in Kosovo as the statement of independence. And after that decision some of the deputies were prosecuted, some were imprisoned, some fled the country. This gave a context to the Belgrade regime, to the Milosevic regime to disband parliament and to close down the media outlets in Kosova, the only television station and Koha Ditore newspaper. Violence was intensified all over the territory of Kosova, and from that time people started to be fired from the more sensitive sectors like the police, the public administration, and other sectors, to continue later with the economic -- the firing of people from economic enterprises and the driving out of students from school premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Just pause there. You're speaking again if you wouldn't mind me saying, very fast. So just take it slowly. And I want to follow on that last part of the last answer where you're dealing with parliament being closed down, television stations being closed down, and so on, and students being driven out. The question I'd like you to deal with is so how did this impinge, impact on your daily life? What did you see going on with your own eyes, just if you could describe, in this period after 1990.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: The citizens of Kosova were being greatly politicised. There was not a single person who wasn't following up developments very closely, because after all, these political developments had a direct impact on each and everyone's life, on my too. So I was one of those who also developed those developments very closely, especially the decision of Kosovo parliament, which was a very welcome decision or a decision which all the citizens of Kosovo had been looking forward to. So there were various sentiments prevailing. It was a kind of euphoria, I would say, which was sweeping over Kosova like the entire Eastern Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Slow down. You are talking very fast. I know you are used to speaking in a very quick manner but it's very difficult for the interpreters and everyone else. I'm sorry to put a brake on it but if you could take a slowly. Sorry. So you were dealing with the fact that it was a kind of euphoria. What I want you to continue from is when there was the shutting down of parliament, the shutting down of the television stations and students being driven out, what happened to you? What did you see actually happening on the streets of Pristina and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: It was something which none of us was clear about. None of us was understanding what was happening, what was going to happen. The Serb response was very violent, but we believed that the federal government wouldn't allow that to continue, wouldn't allow things to go to extreme, and that the situation would change for the better. There were some federal institutions that were still functioning, and we very much hoped that they would find a solution and that these anti-constitutional acts were going to stop and that the situation would change especially after first democratic developments this had just started. So as a young man, I was looking on with sympathy what was happening in parliament. But after what happened, of course, we saw that this couldn't go on but hoped it would change. And we went on with our daily activities as citizens, as students. A new time began in 1990. Everybody was doing something. That is, it was, as I said, a kind of euphoria. People began to freely express their opinions. They saw possibilities of doing things better. We have this phenomenon you know of the blood feuds, of vendetta. It was one of the customs that unfortunately was very dominant in Kosova until of late, and it was at that time what we saw we could do better in the new circumstances. And as a result of this there was an initiative taken by some group of students and formerly political prisoners who started to reconcile blood feuds. At that time some political prisoners were released. They were sentenced because of what they had said orally, publicly. So now nobody would accept to see them in prison, people who had been among the main actors of the events in 1981. So they were released and turned home. They too began to become active in this process of blood reconciliation movement. The entire elite almost subscribed this a movement. The intellectual elite in Kosova. Under the leadership of our honourable professor, a well known processor Anton Ceta, that movement became very active. And in 1991, all our activity was focused on blood reconciliation, blood feud reconciliation, and we managed to reconcile 1.600 families in blood feuds. Maybe the figure is not right, but more or less, and in a way to free these families from their isolation, from their fear of vendettas. As students at that time, we began to act in our respective municipalities trying to do something where we lived. I too was involved in blood feud reconciliation in Malisheve municipality or in some other places. We set up the councils for blood feud reconciliation. The people at that time, the youth -- the people in Kosova had special respect for the students and for what they did. This was more or less when we did. As young people, we ignored. We didn't take seriously what was happening on the part of Serbia, hoping that the federal government would put an end to what was happening if they were really interested in improving the political situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, just before the break if this is the time that Your Honour would seek to have one, could I ask you this: When you were living in Pristina -- just going back to Pristina for a moment. Were you living on your own or were you living with anyone else, any other student or students?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Mostly I lived with my parent [as interpreted] until 1991, 1992, I think, when, as I said, the Serb government drove away the students from their premises, from their dorms, or from public places. Like every other citizen in Pristina, I, too, took in a student to live with me as an act of solidarity, as a response to the pressure exerted by the Serb government, telling them that you might close down the dorms but not our homes. And so for some six months, there were 20 students who lived in the house of my father, students who were unable to live in the dorm. And this was the case with all -- with all the people of Pristina who took in accommodating students for free for them to continue their studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Is there anyone in particular that you remember sharing the house with from that period?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Yes. I remember many of them at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Were any of them to become important later on in the year 1997, 1998? Anybody from that period?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Not in particular. Not at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether you were considering an afternoon break, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mansfield. We have to break at about an hour and a half because of the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We resume at five minutes past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, we're dealing with your university days as a student, but I just want to, as it were, put alongside that a personal development in your life. Is it right that in 1989, just at the beginning of this period, you got married?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And once again if you'd be kind enough just to stand up to your left and mark the village from which your wife came, please. I think it's on that map, and also say the name.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: The village is called Marali.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, if you can just turn the microphone back towards you, the one you just used. I appreciate these children were not all born while you were still at university, but some were. Is it right that you have four children?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: If I may just lead on the dates because there is no controversy here. A son born in 1990; and three daughters, one born in 1993, another in 1995, and the last one in 1999. Are those the correct dates?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, where -- where was your family living? You were at university. Were they living with you in Pristina or were they living in one of the villages with their families?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Most of the time they lived in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry to be precise. Could you say which village that they lived in. It may be obvious ...

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: In my birthplace, in Banje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: How often in this period -- we're still dealing with the 1989 through to 1990, 1991, 1992. How often would you see them? Would you go back at weekends? Just describe what would happen on that.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: During the studies, I would usually go on weekends and during the school breaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Would they ever come to visit you in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated before the break that you graduated in 1994. But before we reach that year, I would like you to deal with other developments at the university. Did there come a time when a form of segregation was imposed at the university?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: This happened back in secondary school before I began my studies at university. At my time, both Serbs and Albanians attended school. However, in 1989, after the propaganda launched by Belgrade regime and after Milosevic created a national programme, a nationalist programme, Serbs began to say that they allegedly were under threat by students, and policemen began to come to schools. In the secondary school where I attended, that was segregated and remained with the Serbs. I refer to the new building where the conditions were better. The majority of students, however, were Albanians. So the entrance of the school was divided. It had two entrances. One the so-called official entrance, which was used for the members of the administration and professors. The other entrance was for students. I don't know who brought those decisions, but the official entrance was now used only for the Serbian students while the usual entrance which students used in the past was now used by Albanian students. In addition, the federal police or the Serb MUP, because it was mostly MUP who acted under the umbrella of the federal police, was present throughout the time in school yards, and this continued to my university days as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: What about the teaching and syllabuses and the use of Albanian language at the university in this period? What happened on those various topics?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: If you could repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to segregation in terms of Serbs being kept separate from Albanians, I'll take them in stages, was the Albanian language permitted as a language for teaching?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: During the secondary school days, yes. We didn't have problems as for the language because we worked under the curriculum of the Kosova government. However, changes occurred after the parliament of Kosova was dispersed, so the curriculum was changed and the Albanians did not accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: After you graduated in 1994, what was your intention? What did you want to do at that time yourself?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: After I graduated in 1994, my intention was to continue with the post-graduate studies. As a result, I enrolled for post-graduate studies in Pristina University, the administration and political branch. At that time, only three or four branches existed for post-graduate studies. I chose this one. I went on lectures and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And presumably this means you remained living in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I'm dealing now with the post-graduate period, 1994 onwards. What about the political situation so far as you understood it, as far as you experienced it, 1994 onwards? What was going on in this period?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: From 1994 onwards, certain developments, important developments, occurred in Kosova, important for the future of the country. First of all, the majority of Kosova had chosen a political leadership that would defend the political interests of Kosova. So everyone took on their assignments. Another important development that occurred in this time was the constitution of Kosova that proclaimed Kosova as a country. This constitution -- I learnt it as a student, and I had an examine on constitution in 1990. The political class in Kosova organised a referendum for the independence of Kosova. The majority of Albanians and other nationalities, except for the Serbs, participated in this referendum. 99 per cent of the citizens declared themselves pro the independence of Kosova. I would like to add that this referendum was held in a way of illegality, without the approval of the authorities. After the referendum results, as it is logical, the political class of Kosova now had a mandate to make the independence of Kosova a reality. And the second step was to organise elections. The general elections aimed at this political class getting a legitimacy by the citizens of Kosova. The response of citizens was massive. They participated massively in the elections, and you can imagine in what circumstances these elections were held and organised. As a result of these elections, a leadership was elected, a parliament, a president. This was the first step towards the institutional building of Kosova. To my opinion, I as a citizen of Kosova participated in all these developments in order to complete my duty towards the country. Now that the situation was stabilised and we had our institutions and we had the people who were elected by the citizens of Kosova to realise our interests --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the witness could speak slower, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could just remind you again as we did before the break. Very difficult, I know, when you have a train of thinking. If you could just take it slowly so the interpreters can keep up. Can I ask you again in relation to this, that is the elections and the institutions, when were the elections?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: The free elections were held in May 1992, while the referendum in September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And who was the leader who was elected as a result of the elections in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: We can't say that a democratic way of life existed in that time. The leadership that had emerged at that time was known to the people, and we didn't have any other alternative, and we didn't need any other alternative at that time. The citizens voted for the Democratic Alliance of Kosova and its leader Ibrahim Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Just moving on from that position, what happened under his leadership in the years that followed 1992 as you were experiencing it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: After these actions, after the conclusion of the first euphoria, after Kosova now had its leadership, people hoped that the question of Kosova would be soon resolved because we had a leadership that would uphold interests of the citizens which in cooperation with the institutions of the federation would see to it. We hoped that after the election we would have the Assembly of Kosova constituted, which was a normal thing. That's why the election was held. But unfortunately, this didn't occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm interrupting. So sorry. I don't mean to interrupt rudely, it's just it is really difficult at the moment to keep up. So if you could bear with us and just speak a little more slowly. It will help everybody. I'm sorry. I have interrupted your train of thought. It was to do with the Assembly of Kosovo as being one of the hopes and aspirations after the election. So if you could just continue with that hope at that point.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: First, I apologise for going so fast. I'll try to be more careful. As I said earlier, the political class in Kosova had called on the people twice to give them a mandate to act, a mandate about the status for Kosova for which they had to work to embody the will of the people. And second, to give them a mandate to -- to make them legitimate leaders and enable them to carry, translate into practice the result of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: The question I want to pose to you is: What is it at that time that you wanted or hoped for Kosovo, you yourself?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: We expected the results to be implemented in practice, to build a new parliament for which we had voted, to have a political class that could find the proper channels, ways to resolve the question of Kosova and the problems we encountered daily, and gradually to reconstruct the institutional life in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And in relation to that, were you hoping for -- I'm going to put the -- various possible alternatives so you can be clear if you had in mind one of these alternatives. Did you want a Kosovo that was independent of all other countries? Did you want a Kosovo that was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. united with another country and, if so, which one and so on? So what did you want? What did you expect?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: I think that at that time, the political class of Kosova came up with various alternatives to the solution of the Kosova issue, probably up to the referendum for independence. I know that through reports I read in the media, what was published there, there were three possible options to the solution of the Kosova and the Albanians' problem in Yugoslavia then. There were three options, as I said, prior to the referendum and the election, as far as I recollect, because at that time Yugoslavia was still intact. One of the options was for Kosova to be independent. The second option was to have a kind of republic which would comprise most of the Albanians distributed in three different republics of Yugoslavia then, that is to have a republic with Albanian majority. And the third alternative was if Kosova would be destroyed, then the option was to join Albania. These were the three options or alternatives put forward by the political class in Kosova at that time. When I say the political class, I mean that in 1990, a coordinating political council was set up which was composed of all the parties, of all the Albanian political parties existed in Kosova at that time, in Macedonia, in Montenegro, and the Albanians in Presheve, Medvegje and Bujanovc. This coordinating council - at leave this is what I presume reading reports in the media about it - its duty was to coordinate the activities, political activities, and to unify the Albanians in Yugoslavia at that time. I'm talking about 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: And at the head of this coordinating council was Mr. Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, which of the options that you've set out which were being put before the public did you prefer or did you not have a preference?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: [In English] I have a problem with the microphones. [Interpretation] I've problem with the microphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Can you hear my questions? Is that all right? I can repeat the last question. We can do a test run on it, which was: Which of the three options, if any of them -- is that all right? All right. The question -- I just want to follow on from your answer. You set out three options put before the public of Kosovo at that time. Did you have yourself a preference for any one of the three or not?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I didn't bother about that at that time. For me it was important that finally Kosova had its political leadership, and for me they knew better what should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, we know that by 1996, you yourself had in fact joined the KLA. So what would be of importance to know is what happened between 1994 and 1996 that caused you to take that step.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: The developments that I mentioned earlier, they had a direct impact on everyone in Kosova and on me, too, since from 1990 to 1994 this leadership had absolute trust, indisputable trust, I would say. They didn't question at all their commitment, and some developments that occurred at that time contributed to the splits and divisions among this political class, especially 1993, 1994. For the first time we started to hear some opposition voices in its ranks which criticised this leadership, political leadership that is. In the context of the Democratic League, splits began to be formed. A great number of those who had contributed to the establishment of this movement began to deflect because of displeasures. One of them was the fact that the parliament of Kosova never set on a very strange [as interpreted] ground, which irritated a number of people. Allegedly they didn't dare sit because of the Serb regime. That was the allegation. On the other hand, the same leadership had been calling to 2 million people to turn out to vote. People were afraid to vote without having the approval of Serbia. That leadership had asked the people to give them the mandate to act. Those deputies were not forced by anyone to be elected. They had undertaken this duty, this risk. So it was inexplicable for people to understand why that parliament didn't start its work. So for them the politics -- there was a stagnated political situation. The situation in general was becoming more difficult. And in my opinion, the active policy finished with the conclusion of the free elections in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Can you go just a little bit more slowly again. I see you are speeding up, or I feel you are. Sorry. Just take a breath. Take a breath. You're talking about the conclusion of the free elections in 1992, so -- and the situation was now stagnating. So the question I want to ask you, did you feel -- you've talked about what other people felt. Did you feel that the political situation after the free elections and so forth and the parliament was stagnating?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Personally, I was looking forward to the establishment of this parliament, and initially we trusted the reasons giving -- given for not forming that parliament. It was then for the first time for us to hear those dissenting voices and to see, to read in the media some alternative reports on the reasons why it didn't sit. Personally, I didn't have any very well-formed opinion. I saw -- I looked at the situation as an ordinary citizen at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, then I'm going to ask you to move forward to 1996. Is that the year in which you did join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Why did you join the KLA in 1996?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Events were linked in Kosova. One led to another. Life became more difficult for all of us. The citizens were seeing an active politics -- from an active politics being turned into a stagnating one. It was a phase where -- where life was very difficult. The political class in Kosova didn't do anything in real terms to bring about any positive changes in the life of the people. People were left to fend for themselves. Those who couldn't fit in the life in slavery, some of them emigrated. A large number of young people did. Another part remained there in the -- hoping that things would change for the better. Another part were looking for alternatives. And developments that occurred, especially after the Dayton agreement, and the frequent instructions given to us by the international diplomacy were -- didn't give us any hope that things would be improved, that there would be a solution, a short-term solution for the country. Indeed, there were some rumours in the international diplomacy which said that the situation in Kosova is calm and we shouldn't hurry to find another solution. There were some who said that in Dayton are only those who have fought, and that in Kosova things are developing properly. Kosova was looked upon only as a case where there were violation of human rights. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want to stop you at that stage just to put it in again a context. The Dayton agreement was in December 1995. Were there representatives of Kosovo present in the talks that led to that agreement, so far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: No, there were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Was that an issue that concerned people like yourself in Kosovo, that you were excluded from those talks?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Of course. This was a turning point, in my view, in the way people in Kosova began to think. Dayton was an important event. It was, in our view, a defeat or an agreement that disregarded everything we had done until then regarding our political definition as a country. It was -- it was looked as another manipulation that was done by the political leadership. In fact, people had great trust in that leadership and they didn't look for other truths. Then only heard what that leadership told them. But after this development, people started to realise that the truth was different, that the reality was different, and they started to look for other alternatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you some practical questions. Where did you join the KLA? I mean, was it an office in Pristina or a home somewhere? Where did you do it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to know certain colleagues, students in the 1990s. Sometime in late 1992, I met Rexhep Selimi. He lived in the apartment of a friend of my parent, and he then came to live in my apartment. Later on, if I'm not mistaken, we lived about two years in the same apartment, and sometime in August 1996, in a conversation we had, we discussed these developments because at that time the KLA came public with certain communiques, and we of course were part of that -- of those who didn't know, who were not well informed what was true and what was not true. In these conversations, Rexhep Selimi said to me that the KLA as an organisation existed and that he was a member of the KLA. He said that if I wanted to, I could join the KLA to help it. I said to him that they could count on my assistance, meaning providing shelter and other facilitating things, especially in my birthplace. So this was my first contact with the KLA, although I knew Rexhep Selimi before. Until that moment, I didn't know that he was a member of the KLA. From this time on, I felt as being a member of the KLA, meaning from August 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, a series of questions arise. First one: What did you understand were the objectives of the KLA in August 1996?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: The main objective was to prepare a liberating war for Kosova in order to realise what people wanted and what people voted for with the objective of what I had learnt at school in order to fulfil the constitutional obligations that the Kosova parliament had. So this was the objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Did you understand that there was any targeted time for this war?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: What do you mean by targeted time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, you indicated in your answer that you -- that the objective was to prepare a liberating war for Kosovo. Did anyone have in mind when that process would actually begin? In other words, the process of taking up arms to secure liberation.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: No. At that time, nothing concrete regarding dates came up. This was a process. This was a movement towards engagement. Certain developments had already started in this direction. The KLA had undertaken some actions. And with this preparation - I mean mobilisation of people - at this time, at this phase, the circumstances were different. At that time, I didn't even ask about these things because I thought these were matters that the Kosova institutions were well-familiarised with and because I thought that someone else was to look after these things. And as all other citizens, my obligation was to fulfil my duties as a citizen of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: You indicated that you would be prepared to help. The example you gave was shelter. Now, in 1996, did you in fact help in any practical ways that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: At that time, from conversations with Rexhe, I recall that these were their demands. I found out that they had a need for shelter, and we discussed about people, about different activities, propaganda for new alternatives, to search for new alternatives without mentioning the KLA. Concretely, there was an occasion when Rexhep and another friend stayed with me in Banje. I provided shelter for them. I stayed with them. Even in my apartment now I knew that there was a KLA member staying in my apartment. So these were my main activities at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And you mentioned also that the KLA undertook certain actions, you call them, some actions. Again, were these actions in this period 1996 and, if so, can you recall what the actions were?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: I think that the communique had just been published, and in it certain actions were described, a guerrilla attack launched by KLA members against some Serbian police stations. At that time, you could read about this in daily media through the communiques, KLA communiques.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Were you yourself involved in any way in the -- in assisting with guerrilla actions from 19 -- from August of 1996 onwards?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't have the opportunity then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: We're approaching the beginning of 1997, and something very important happened in January 1997. Would you please describe what that was.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
