utterances.text: I would like to mention that before January, if I'm not mistaken, sometime in September, October 1996, Rexhep Selimi began to act illegally because he was -- his identity was discovered by the Serbian police. He was forced to leave Pristina. Now, in 1997, in late January, the Serbian state security forces undertook a general operation of arrests. More than 100 people were arrested. Three were killed as members of the KLA. I was -- my name was on the list of the persecuted persons. Fortunately, I was not at home that night. I was staying at a friend's house when a considerably great police force encircled my house. They searched my house. They were looking for me. As I was not at home, they arrested my parent. The following day, they also arrested my brother as he came back from Pristina to Malisheve.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Which brother was that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: And I was fortunate not to be arrested since I was not there that night. Demir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Demir was the brother. And which of your parents was detained?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: My father.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I just want to deal with those two before we move on in your own story. For how long was your father detained or arrested? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Approximately six months, for six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And so far as you're aware, was he maltreated during that six-month period in custody?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Yes. He still suffers the consequences of the maltreatment to this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: So far as again you are aware, had he done anything to merit being arrested?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: He had nothing to do with any action, with nothing at all. He was arrested just for being my father and for having me in his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: May I move to your brother Demir. Was he charged with any offence by the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: He was accused of being a member of the KLA, and he was sentenced to eight years' imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And so -- again I'm just dealing with Demir for the moment. When was he released from the eight-year sentence?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Demir was released in 2001, after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: So after the war. And in his case, was -- as far as you are aware, was he maltreated by the Serb authorities during the time he was kept in prison?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: I think it was a miracle how he escaped these tortures that were in force in 1997 and 1998, especially exercised on those who were accused of such activities as my brother Demir was. I didn't see him personally, but these were descriptions provided by my family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, the particular date, if I can just put this to you, of the arrest and the search was January the 31st, 1997. Are you able to say that that is the correct date that this all happened?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And when was it that you learnt of the particular forms of mistreatment that occurred to Demir? Was it after his release in 2001 or at some earlier stage?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: This was in 2000, when my mother managed to visit him at the Nis prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And can you recall the nature of the mistreatment that your mother recounted to you?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: They used electroshocks against him, and they deprived him of food, beat him up and such things. They left him hungry for a long time. When my mother went to visit him in 2000, she didn't recognise him and some others she knew because of the fact that they had been famine [as interpreted]. They had lost a lot of weight. It was only when he stood up that -- and called her that she recognised him. Then we started sending him food from Kosova in 2000. And as my mother described him, this was the same with other mothers who visited their sons. According to her description, he didn't weight more than about 30 kilos at that time, when normally he's a well-built young man. He was like this before he was arrested. And as Demir told my mother, they had not eaten properly and were constantly tortured by the Serb authorities. Demir is one of the eyewitnesses of the massacre in Dubrava during which more than 260 Albanian prisoners got killed. At that time, we didn't know about such developments. We found out after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And when had that massacre occurred?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: The massacre occurred sometime in April, May 1999 during the airstrikes when the Serbs fired directly at the prisoners, shot at them, killing some of them, injuring some others. Some others managed to escape. Among them was my brother. People don't speak about that. He doesn't speak about that. Sorry. There are 3, 400 living people who have seen with their own eyes what happened at that time. But Demir doesn't like to talk much about that. At least with me he didn't discuss it very much. After his release from prison, we didn't stay much together because of my political engagements. It's very rarely that we met and talked like two brothers do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: May I take you back to January the 31st, 1997, when that sequence of events began. You weren't at home when the police raid occurred. What did you decide to do after that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: At that time, you had to be psychologically -- psychically ill or mentally ill or mad to go and hand yourself over to the Serbs knowing what to expect you. I was fortunate not to be at home at that time. I hid myself somewhere and then went to people, to families I knew well, with which we had family links, and tried to make arrangements to flee Kosova. That was the only way to escape falling into the Serb hands. If you allow me, I will speak -- I will say a detail. I heard from my mother about what happened in the night of the 31st. The mother came to the village where I was taken that night as a guest, and when I heard about my father being arrested, I thought to surrender myself in order for the Serbs to release my father. But my mother didn't allow me to do that. She insisted on me not handing myself over to the Serbs but to flee the country. And this is what I did. Then upon second thoughts, I realised at that it was better to flee than to surrender to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want to ask you before we leave Kosovo, though, about your wife, and by this stage there are three children, one born in 1990, another in 1993, and another in 1995. What did you feel about their situation in view of what was happening to you?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: The situation was not an easy one, of course, but we could expect it from Serbia. This was something that didn't happen only to my family. Many other people had suffered. Thousands of people had suffered. Some had been killed. So that was not an extraordinary thing for me. Of course we didn't like it, but it was a reality. We couldn't help it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: You mentioned that you stayed or, rather, hid with families that you knew. Can you just indicate -- I don't want the names of the families, but can you just indicate where they were situated in Kosovo, the places where you hid?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: I might mention their names as well. There is no problem. I had stayed with our in-law in Carralluke village, with my brother-in-law, and this is where my mother found him -- found me, sorry. Then I went on to stay with some other nephews and there I contacted a friend of mine who tried to find ways for us to leave Kosova. I stayed afterwards at a family in Panorc village. My uncle had his sister-in-law living with that family. We were good friends. It was a family member with whom I had constant contacts. I knew him very well. So I kept changing places, coming closer to the border with Albania. After a time, this friend of mine who could move freely all over Kosova, he had arranged for me to meet and to leave for Albania. During all the time I was underground, it was a time when even my family didn't know my whereabouts because the Serb police went daily to look for me at my family. They started to maltreat residents from my neighbourhood, to imprison them, relatives of mine as well like the person with whom I had stayed that night in Carralluke. They took him, Isak, and his two sons. This is what they did to all the people they thought had links with me or knew about my whereabouts. But I kept Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. changing places without telling my family where I was. So I managed to escape then. For this I have to thank also the people, the families that sheltered me and escorted me from one place to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: You mentioned in that answer or referred to nephews. Were any of the nephews or relatives in Klecka that you hid at that time?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, because I said we have a large family. I may tell you that the entire Klecka can be identified with that family. It's a family where I have six nephews. It's a large family, well-to-do economically, with a good reputation on a national scale. And it was my right hand, I would say. For everything I've had to give me economic assistance or for any problem we might have had, these people offered to help me. During the time I was a student they helped me economically to finish my studies, me and my family. So the first thing I did was to turn for help to this family. And they were living in a remote, mountainous village, so you can live there without drawing the attention of -- of people. So I was certain I could stay with them for as long as I wished, and from there I could think of doing something else. I have to tell you, if you allow me, Your Honours, that at that time it was very difficult to shelter people like me because you might suffer. Your family might suffer. You could expect that to be done by very close relatives of yours. But that family, as I said, were willing to defy the danger and to shelter me. Some of my relatives, as I said, suffered because of that. They went to gaol or were maltreated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, you've described, as it were, inching your way or getting closer to the border with Albania. Did you in fact cross into Albania at some stage?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: I don't know if the village of Panorc is on the map, but from this village I walked without stopping. This is a village on the borderline between Malisheve and Klina municipality. So I walked without stopping together with a friend of mine up to the border with Albania and -- to Albania, in fact, to the nearest village in Albania. The journey took us about 35 to 40 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: There's the second map there on the board, and I wonder if you would kind enough with a felt pen just to -- if you can find roughly the route you took on foot across the Albania border and just mark it, if you wouldn't mind.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: The village of Panorc, as I said, is somewhere here. We used off-roads, so it is difficult for me to find them, but this is approximately the route.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: That's fine. Just an approximation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe hard copies of this map are available and will be before you, and what I intend to do, if I may, is when the markings are finally finished, if these can become exhibits. We haven't quite finished with this map either for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: When you crossed the border into Albania, had you any idea where you were intending to go after that? Stay in Albania, go to another country, or what?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, my sole intention at that time was to leave and to avoid the danger from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: So what did you do at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: After this friend that was with me, as he knew some people there, his name is Ragip Shala. We studied together in Pristina. He had gone to Albania before during his economic activities. He had some friends in Tirana, and together with him we stayed in an apartment there. We contacted his friends. They helped us find accommodation, and nothing else. We were just waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And what were you, if I may ask, waiting for? What did you hope would happen?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Simply, we were waiting for information, what was going on in Kosova with our families. Then we were waiting also for the engagements by -- at that time, to tell you the truth, I was thinking of even continuing my studies in Tirana, my post-graduate studies, but unfortunately after I stayed there for 20 days or a month Albania entered a crisis. This is known by March riots. So at that time, we didn't see a short improvement, a short-time improvement of the situation in Albania, and we didn't see a perspective for us. So in contact with certain persons there we decided to leave Albania and to go to Switzerland. The situation in Albania was chaotic because of the developments that occurred due to the March riots.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Why Switzerland? Was there some particular reason?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: The only reason was that this was a country that I had visited in the past in 1989, and I also had family there. I had some of these nephews from Klecke village living in Switzerland. So I thought I could count on their help for anything I needed. This was the main reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Did you travel alone to Switzerland?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: No. We were a group of seven or eight, maybe even six, I don't know. We all travelled together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Any of the six or seven individuals who returned with you or you met again later or are they all people that disappeared after that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Out of these persons, I only know the person who was with me. These were people who were fleeing Albania or other countries, people that I didn't know. I don't know even where their destination was, where they were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And where did you end up in Switzerland?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: I went to Geneva, and I applied for political asylum at a reception centre. Then they sent us to Lausanne and I settled in the canton of Vaud in Lausanne.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Were you granted asylum?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Yes, after three or four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And were there people in the place where you settled in the canton of Lausanne, were they relatives or friends or unknown? In other words, what were the premises where you stayed?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: The Swiss government offered us accommodation. They offered accommodation and organised accommodation of the asylum seekers. I lived in their settlements. One of them lives in Lausanne, one in Fribourg and in the surrounding area with my nephews.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: During this time, had you had contact with your wife and children back in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: For some three or four months or even more, we didn't have any contact at all. After this time, I contacted them by phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And were they surviving all right in this period or were there difficulties? What was the position for them?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: There were problems, because none of us who could provide for the family was in the house. Demir was imprisoned, my brother was imprisoned, my youngest brother at that time Florim was at that time in Germany. He was working there. My uncle was almost paralysed. It was my mother who was trying to cope with this situation. The Serbian government had placed Demir in Pristina prison and my father in Prizren prison to make it impossible for my mother to visit had them both, because the visiting time was at the same time and at the same hour so it was impossible for her to visit them both. These were really difficult -- this was really difficult situation for my family and other families in Kosova. We were not alone in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Did you manage to find work in Switzerland?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, there was no need for me to work because my relatives didn't want me to work. They had a good political -- economical situation, and they had worked in Switzerland for a long time. As they helped us in the past, they wanted to help me now as well. However, I was resolute to find a work because I wanted to provide for myself alone and for my family as well. So with the help of certain friends of mine, I found a work, a job in a hotel in Switzerland in a tourist place, Montreux, and I worked as an assistant in that hotel for three or four months. After this time, I had some health problems. I was admitted to a hospital for a short time. I underwent a minor surgery, so I stopped working because my nephews insisted on me stopping.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is not working.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: If we can pause just for a minute to -- can you hear the questions I'm asking?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Up to this time, I did hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Mansfield, that might be a convenient time, then, and the difficulty can be attended to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- during the break. We will resume just after ten minutes to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: May I just ask whether the -- they're all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, we're in Switzerland. You've dealt with a number of areas. One which I want to ask about in particular is whether you maintained contact with the KLA while you were there.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Will you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. You were in Switzerland. I want to ask you whether while you were there you maintained contact with the KLA back in Kosovo or its representatives or people who were connected with it in Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: After I settled in Switzerland, I didn't have contacts with the KLA or its members because it was impossible for me to have such contacts in Switzerland, because even if there were people like me, they wouldn't say like me. I didn't say that I had contacts with the KLA for the only reason that the KLA was in Kosova. And for people being outside Kosova, it didn't make any sense to tell them this. The only contact or link I had with KLA was in mid-summer, if I am not mistaken. It was Rexhep Selimi who sent me a greeting, a letter of greetings with his brother. But there was nothing in that letter other than his greetings and his expression of pleasure at my escaping Serb forces. As to other contacts, while I was in Switzerland I want to tell you that the Albanian diaspora in Switzerland and in the other countries in the west was organised in various political organisations. I was fortunate that in the place of my residence in Lausanne, I became acquainted with some people among whom I would like to single out Bardhyl Mahmuti and Ramadan Avdiu and Adem Grabovci. These three people, former political prisoners. Bardhyl and Ramadan were continuing post-graduate studies at Lausanne and Geneva universities. Since we were very close, Bardhyl used to come often to visit me or invite me to his family because he was there with his family. They were members of the leadership of the Kosova Popular Movement for Switzerland, and they were open supporters. That was the source for the organisation of the KLA, actually, that movement. They were engaged in political activities to make the KLA known to diaspora and for diaspora help this formation that is the KLA. I also started to join their activities. At that time in Switzerland, like in other countries of the west, some informative rallies, we call them, began to inform diaspora of the existence of the KLA as a first phase. And as a second phase we started to collect, raise money for it, the national liberation war, through the fund Homeland Is Calling. And so gradually I, as I said, became active in such activities even though I was not a member of the Kosova Popular Movement, I was a sympathiser of this movement, and a sympathiser of those people who had devoted their life to the question of the liberation of the homeland. And so started my activity in meetings with the diaspora. Becoming acquainted with such people for me was very important, because through such people I managed to -- to get to know things about the life of the diaspora. They were thinking various activities organised by them. They were people who had left Kosova for -- since many years ago. Some of them didn't have a sense of reality in Kosova, about development there. I want to point out that even though they had left Kosova for many years, such people had never broken off relations with their country. In various ways and forms they tried to assist, to contribute to the movement in Kosova. They assisted their families and the political activities. So I looked at them with admiration. In Switzerland they had all the possibilities to lead a good life, but even though they had the possibilities the life they were leading was very simple, very modest, because all the money they could spare they had put to the Kosova cause. Some of them had left, as I said, for many years ago, and for me it was the first time to met some of them. Some of them were former political prisoners. That was good experience for me. I want to stress that despite their willingness, despite their sacrifice for their country, despite their interest in Kosova, there were some who because they had left Kosova, as I said, for a long time, they found it difficult to grasp the developments and the realities in Kosova and sometimes they had differing -- different views about developments there. My meetings with them, my constant stay with Bardhyl Mahmuti and Ramadan Avdiu helped me a lot because these two were open-minded people. They had left Kosova at a later phase, and they had been integrated in the Swiss society, and they were more informed about the reality in Kosova, and together we thought of doing something good for the country to sensitise the public among the diaspora about the new circumstances created in Kosova, about the new forces established, about Kosova embarking on a new phase of political developments, that the so-called political efforts had failed and that Milosevic was the main argument; that the war in Bosnia and Croatia had already proven that Milosevic would not -- under no circumstances give Albanians of Kosova their rights or accept Kosova to get away from his federation without the Albanians doing something themselves. As of 1995, in my opinion, Albanians had been following that slogan "Do what you can on your own," but none of them had done any serious -- had made any serious efforts to do something about the country, to change the situation, and from that time I continued my activities in Switzerland, taking part in rallies and so on, and raising funds as I said earlier. I want to say that in none of the rallies there was anyone, at least that I knew of, being a member of the KLA, because there was no KLA in Switzerland. Those who were KLA members were in Kosova. I continued this activity until I returned to Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want to come to that point of when you return, which we know is in the spring of 1998. Now, my first question here is: Why did you decide to return?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: There are many reasons for that, one of them being that I had voluntarily subscribed to such an initiative. I was convinced that this was an attempt made in an organised way. I felt it my moral obligation to join the KLA. Nobody forced me to do that. What affected my haste to return to Kosova was the March events. Hadn't it been for the March events, I would have returned upon the first opportunity to continue my activity. But the fact that accounted for my quick decision was the Likoshan, Qirez, and Prekaz massacres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Were these massacres something that you read about in the newspapers in Switzerland or was on television or came through friends? How did you hear about them?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: The first time we heard about that was through the media outlets. It was a tragedy that could not be kept a secret, especially foreign radio broadcasts, which were the only window to us -- for us to communicate with Kosova, like the BBC service in Albanian, the VOA in Albania, the Deutsche Welle, and the Albanian television had informed us of what had happened. There was a daily newscast for Kosova broadcast by the Albanian television. These were the sources which informed us of what happened. But people also communicated with one another through the telephone. We kept links with our families. So the news spread like wildfire. But as I said, it was BBC, CNN, all the most important international television stations broadcast that news.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Did you decide to return on your own or with a group of people?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: I decided on my own to return. I contacted Adem Grabovci, who was an act advice of the fund Motherland Calls. I knew that he went often to Albanian. At that time I had not left Switzerland. I couldn't. I knew that that guy had the links that could help me go from Albania to Kosova, and I called him once to find someone for me in Albania to help me go to Kosova, and he told me that there are other people who want to go. And so I decided to go back to Kosova -- sorry, to Albania. There are two other people who have always helped us form a friendship. I mean Ismet Jashari, aka Kumanova, and the family relative of mine and a friend with whom I went to school in Banje. His name is Haxhi Shala. To tell you the truth, those people knew that I was going to Kosova. They didn't know at least they didn't hear me say that I was a member of the KLA. No one when I was in Switzerland knew about that. I was ashamed to say I was a member of the KLA being in Switzerland, because for that I had to be in Kosova. So I told them I'm going to Albania. I have some thing to do there. They might have said something. And they asked to come with me to Albania. I tried to escape them, so to say, but it was impossible. They insisted on coming with me, and they came with me. I thought that after I went to Albania I would find a way to go to -- to return to Kosova. My nephews with whom I lived in Switzerland, I told them I was going to London. I told them that I'm going to London for some activities related to this fund and that I would be missing for some days. So I had made sure that they didn't know where I was going, because it was dangerous. It was simply dangerous that word might spread that we -- before us arriving in Kosova people knew that we would be going there. We had to be careful to protect our families. And this is what I did, together with these two people that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Did anyone in Kosovo know that you were returning?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: No. No, absolutely not. It was beyond imagination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you straight to Albania. You flew, is this correct, to Tirana?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Yes. From Zurich airport I flew to than a there were many Albanians on that plane. Among them there were people whom I knew later, people who also wanted to go to Kosova. Some of them I met when we approached the border. And this is how we went to Albania, to Tirana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Once you arrived in Tirana, which is in fact marked at least slightly off the map of the second map, bottom left-hand corner as you look at it, south-west corner, once you got to Tirana, how did you travel to the border?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: First I want to tell you that Adem Grabovci received me at the airport with these other guys. He had gone to Albania two days before me from the Rinas airport we went to Tirana. We stayed one night in Tirana. Adem had rented an apartment. Maybe it's of interest for You Honoured Judges that after we arrived in Tirana things were more or less clear, the reason for my trip to Albania. Haxhiu and Ismet Jashari whose families didn't know about their trip, so their wives and children didn't know where they were going, they knew simply that they were going to Albania for four or five days. Then I was obliged to tell them that I'm going to Kosova and that you may stay in Albania for four or five days as you wish, and then when you go back to Switzerland, please don't tell anyone that we have gone to Kosova. Tell them that we remained in Albania and from Albania will go to a western country. But Ismet and Haxhi insisted that they knew from the first moment that I was not going to remain in Albania and that they too were determined to accompany me to Kosova. Despite my insistence that they go back to Switzerland to their family for a short time to see what would happen because in fact we didn't know what was going on in Kosova at the time. And personally, I didn't know where I was going, where I was staying, what would happen after that. And I didn't want to take these two along with me. We were going to an unknown, let's say, place, towards an unknown fate. So I felt that they were not prepared to face unexpected situations, because from outside it might be easier for you to have an idea of the situation, but when you go there on the ground, the situation might be different. But these two guys were determined. They wanted to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. come with me no matter what. And this is what we did. And on the next day, Adem told us to leave at 8.00, to -- we travelled by bus, kombi bus it was called. We travelled towards the border. He told us that in the border there are people who will escort us. There will be some activists of this Homeland Calls fund who had come from different countries and they also were determined to go to Kosova. So we would form a group and together we would enter Kosova, he told us. On the next day at 8.00 we left. We got on the bus and set out to Fokukus [phoen] from Tirana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could you again, on the second map on the board, just indicate with a different pen from the one you've used already so we can distinguish the route out and the route back can you indicate on that with a felt pen, some colour you haven't used, the point on the Albania border where you crossed back into Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: What colour have you used so we know -- black. Black. Yes. I want to ask you -- now, the place where you crossed the border, was it a border crossing or was it a little-known track? What was it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: It was a little-known track, I would say, a track used by shepherds mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, did you cross it on foot or in a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: From the place we left and to the place of our destination, we travelled on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And who is the "we"? Who is with you as you cross the border?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: When we arrived at Krume by using different roads, we were about ten persons in the van, and some others joined us on the way. At the place where we stopped we were about 30. We spent the night there and the entire day, the following day. In the evening we travelled. At that time, of course, I didn't know the names of the persons who were travelling with me, but I learned these names later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And who were they?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Maybe I cannot remember all of them at this moment, but I will do my best to mention all of them. I will start with Fehmi Lladrovci's name. I didn't know him from before. It was the first time that I saw him. I will continue with the name of his wife, Xhevat. I didn't know her either. Then Bekim Berisha, whom I didn't know from before. I don't know the name of one person, but his pseudonym was CD. I know that he came from the Llap region. These two persons came from Croatia. Then Sami Lushtaku. I didn't know him to that moment. There was also Sahit Jashari. I knew him from before. I had met him once in Kosova in 1996 in his house. There was -- there were two Geci brothers. I don't remember their names at the moment. And one of their nephews. Then myself, Ismet Jashari, Haxhi Shala, then Xhema, Xhem Gashi. I didn't know him until that time. Then Shukri Buja. I knew him from before. I had met him in Switzerland. I had met him once or twice in some rallies. I worked as a journalist. I met him in a rally in Zurich. Then Hashim Thaqi, the president of the Democratic Party, and a person whom I didn't know by name at that time but whom I had seen in Switzerland, and I had met with him once or twice there. His pseudonym was Luan. And then Kadri Veseli . I didn't know him from before. There were also some young men from the Dukagjini area, but I don't remember their names or pseudonyms. These were the persons whom I saw at that time. I would like to add, if possible, that Bekim Berisha, known by the pseudonym Abeja at that time, when we went to the place where we spent the night, he gave me the impression of being a military officer because he had participated in the Croatian war together with the person with the pseudonym CD, and they had military experience. I know that some of the weapons arrived that night, an automatic rifle. We began to clean the weapons, and he started to teach other persons how to operate the rifle, because 70 or 80 per cent of those there didn't even know how to open a rifle. They were young men. They hadn't completed their military service. We discussed the way we were going to travel and how we were going to do it, and they also said that if someone was not prepared to cope with that journey then they should return now and not at a later stage. So basically this is what was discussed that night. The following day, in the evening, we travelled. I would like to say that throughout this time, we stayed with a family in a house on the Albanian-Kosova border. They had deserted the house, and probably one of these friends had rented their house. At around 8.00 or 9.00 p.m., we all got on our backs a military bag, about 25 or 30 kilogrammes loaded with ammunition, bombs, and we set off towards the border. As I said, the column was led by those who were experienced, Abeja or Bekim and CD. As for the journey, there were two from Albania and one from Kosova, a young man who was usually there waiting and escorting people at the border. And this is how we set off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, the question that should be asked at this point is: Was anyone in charge of your group?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, from a military point of view, if we can call it a military point of view, from the way they communicated with us as a group you could tell that Bekim and Fehmi Lladrovci were the two persons who had the most of experience. As for leadership, there was Hashim and Kadri. I can say that this was the group that was kind of a leadership to our group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: At that point when you crossed the border, did you have any idea where you were going in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Well, at that time it was said that we were going in the Drenica area. We didn't know the exact place where we were going. I think that except for Hashim and maybe Fehmi Lladrovci, nobody else knew where we were going, but we were all knew that we were going to Drenica. We didn't know the exact place or the exact village where we were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Who had decided Drenica was the destination?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Well, it was clear at that time there was no other place you could go to except for Drenica. That was the place where the fighting was going on. That was the only place that could have had a KLA place and -- a KLA base and a place where the KLA soldiers could be assigned to. When I'm speaking of Drenica, I do not refer to the entire area of Drenica. I'm referring to some villages in the Prekaz area, some villages that had entered combat at that time. So we all knew that we were going in Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry to persist a bit. It may be important, I don't know. But did somebody, one of you, even though you all realised that's where you were going, did one of you decide that was the obvious place to go, or was this generally discussed and agreed amongst you this was the only place to go? How did it happen?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: There was no special decision. People were just going there to join the KLA, and the only address that you could go to and join the KLA at that time was Drenica. Whoever set off for joining the KLA, they -- their destination was Drenica. As I said, the people who were leading us during that journey, they were heading there and they knew better because they had information from inside where to go. You should consider the fact that we didn't have any exact information what was going on in Kosova, where Serb forces were positioned or where the KLA members were positioned. We didn't know what was the journey we were going to undertake. So those were the people who knew exactly, who knew the accurate place where to go in Drenica. There were also others who did not come to Drenica but stopped at other places. Some stopped at their birthplace, some who had been persecuted in the past. Now maybe it's good to make a distinction here. I just remembered. We in a way were searched for by the Serb forces. So for us there existed only one way, one address, Drenica. For some others who were not -- for whom the Serbian forces had no knowledge of, they could stop in their birthplaces and visit their families. I with like to say that the majority of us went to Likovc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: If you wouldn't mind, we've got the place where you crossed the border. Could you as far as you can with the same pen that you've just used mark on that second map the route you just had to get to Likovc. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Approximately this is the route.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. I gather it's on the monitors now. I don't know whether you have it or not. Thank you. You've marked the route. How long did it take you to go that distance?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: In hours, about 75 hours. I would like to say that the journey took place at night and only at night. Whenever -- at dawn we would plan to find a shelter place in the mountains and shelter there until the evening, and at night we would proceed on foot and so on. During the day we would shelter. At night we would proceed with our journey. The terrain was very difficult. It was March, and the mountains on the Kosova Albanian border are very difficult to pass, especially at winter. There was snow up to a metre, a metre and a half on these mountains, so it was very difficult for us to travel through this terrain. Then we encountered difficulties inside Kosova since we had to use invisible, so to say, roads, off-roads. We had to pass rivers as Drini Ibar River is, on foot. We would get wet and then wait to dry and it was really, really difficult. So it took us about 75 hours, approximately 75 hours to reach Likovc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And was something showing you the way?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Yes. At all times we had persons who were leading us, especially in such circumstances. You cannot manage a journey without having some who know the terrain. There were two persons who had travelled that road and who knew the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: How many were left in your group by the time you arrived in Likovc?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I didn't show much interest to find out the number, but I believe that we were 24 or 25, we who arrived at Likovc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And where did you go in Likovc?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: We arrived around 3.00 in the morning. We separated. I know that we met with Musa Jashari and Rexhep Selimi in Likovc. Musa had gone out to wait for his brother Zahid, and after the tragedy that had occurred in Prekaz, their family had suffered losses. Their mother and father were killed as well as other members of the family. So he had gone out to wait for his brother who had been away from Kosova for a long time. I know that Musa took us to a house where he was staying after he had left Prekaz. So we spent that night there where Musa was staying together with some family members of his. Some villagers had given them part of their house after the Prekaz events. So we spent that night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Did you personally have any weapons or ammunition with you?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Yes. As all the others had, I also had an automatic rifle of Yugoslav make, and I had a military bag filled with different ammunition, which was about 20 or 25 kilos in weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Likovc?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: I think we stayed approximately seven or ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: In that time, did you discover whether the KLA as an organisation had set up all kinds of points, had established a structure? I mean, what did you discover about the KLA at this first arrival?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: When we arrived at Likovc, the next day we wanted to see where we stood, what the situation was. We wanted to face the reality that existed there at that time. We couldn't wait to meet KLA members and to meet the people there. We had that western opinion, an imagination that was quite different from the reality there. We met with people who didn't even have uniforms. Some of them had a rifle, some didn't. And we were looking at them with sympathy, and they were looking back at us with sympathy and hope. There it was obvious to us that the reality was different from that of our imagination. After the developments in Prekaz, the situation was extremely difficult, and simply for those who hoped or who in a way were optimistic about the developments inside Kosova, what we saw on the first day in Likovc was really disappointing. It was not what we expected. We faced quite a different situation, a situation that we could not even imagine before entering Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: So what was the reality that you discovered on the first day?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: The reality was that in a small village of Drenica, in Likovc, you could see 15, 20 people armed within the village, people who were still under the influence of the recent battle of Prekaz. They were all talking about the tragedy, its consequences. People were very scared. The situation in the village was very tense. They expected some retaliation action by the Serbs, and they were not capable of protecting their village. And the number of the KLA members was very small. I went to visit a point which was set up to protect the village. I remember there were about 20 people there. I remember a teacher, Rifat Musliu [phoen], he's a hero now. If I not mistaken about his name. He had a hunting gun, two automatic rifles and a few other rifles. There were some 16 people wearing some KLA insignia. The situation was really grave. We didn't see more than 15, 16 people then. We went to various villages to rest -- to homes in the village to rest. On the next day, we started to talk with villagers. We could see that they -- their only hope was in us. So the reality we found was really very sad. I may be wrong, but I don't think I saw more than 200 soldiers altogether, in all those areas. When I'm talking about the number, I'm talking about the whole region, even outside Drenica. The situation was very, very critical. Fighting was going on in some villages near Prekaz. People were unarmed. They lacked munitions. Serbia had dealt a very heavy blow following the murder of the legendary commander, and the outcomes were very obvious for everybody to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: What did you decide you could do, in fact, therefore?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: We stayed there for several days, and we could talk to people every day, to soldiers. Now we saw some civilians coming and joining the KLA, people who wanted to defend the village. We could talk with them. We could become acquainted with some members of the KLA. Two of the KLA members had been injured in Likoshan and Qirez actions. They were being treated in a room there. Some medical assistance was being administered to them. Dr. Fadil was the person. And we saw people who came to visit the injured persons, and they recounted new developments. So we saw that there was no reason for us to remain there. People were very poor. They couldn't even feed us. What could we do in a small hamlet with 20, 30 village -- households? They wanted to help us but we couldn't stay there at the crossroads of the village, walk around, talk with people. We told them about life abroad. They all looked up at us waiting for us to tell them what to do. So in a way they had thought we had come there that -- because we knew what was going to happen. It was -- for us it was a confrontation with the truth. We had expected something else. They had expected something else. So both sides had expected different things. So they were under the constant pressure and threat of the Serb forces. I wanted to go to my municipality to see what I could do there in Malisheve municipality, at least to provide economic assistance to them and to expand the activity of the KLA to other zones, because the purpose of Serbia was to localise the war. Even within Drenica the Serb forces had managed to divide Drenica and to minimise the war within six, seven villages. So seeing all this, I went to Rexhep Selimi whom I met every day and with whom we [as interpreted] talked. We couldn't ask because the situation -- the information was considered secret. So we just talked in general. I went to him, to Rexhep, since -- whom I considered as a friend mostly, to tell him that there was no need for me to stay here. I don't see the point of my remaining here and that I wanted to go to my municipality and try to do something there, recruit people, to expand the activity to other municipalities. Because if we -- if we remain here, what shall we do? Rexhep thought that everyone could shoot, act, whatever we could. So for us it would be better for us to go back to our native villages and where we could find more easily accommodation and food. And this is what we did. After one or two days, I tried to establish some contact with someone from Malisheve, to find some people I knew. Then Haxhi, who was not wanted by the Serb forces, he had been working in Switzerland for one year, and he was a person who could go freely -- legally, I might say so, to his home. And he went to Malisheve and arranged for our transit from Likovc to Malisheve engaging a cousin of his to come and pick us up at a certain place where we had agreed. And after two days, I met Rexhe again. Hashim was present at the meeting. I was prepared to go to my native village. Hashim told me that if it's possible -- I forgot to mention the name of Agim Bajrami who was among the group of 30 persons. So he asked me if I could get Shukri and Agim with us so that they could pass from Malisheve to their respective municipalities. So almost all of us who were there went back to our respective municipalities. I offered my, of course, help to Shukri. He came with us. He ate with us in the same place. So I offered him the same safety I had for myself. I couldn't guarantee him more. So they were supposed to come with us, and we promised to help them go back to their municipalities. Lipjan and Stimlje were their respective municipalities. Agim was supposed to go to Kacanik and this is what we did. Shukri came and told Hashim that he would go together with me to Malisheve, and we set off at about 9.00 on the next day in the next evening. Two villagers escorted us. They gave us a lift with their car up to the main road, Pristina-Peja road to Mlecan village. Then after that, we walked on foot. We passed the main road and headed to Vermice village. Because it was very late, we decided to stay over in Vermice with some family members of Haxhi. It was someone called Jupa, I remember. I don't remember his last name. At that house we stayed that night. In fact, it was his brother's home. We stayed there also during the next day, and Haxhi -- then on the next day Haxhi went to met his cousin to come and pick us up or along this Orlat-Malisheve-Terpeze asphalt road. And in the evening of the second day we, the five of us, set off for the place where two other people were supposed to meet us. From Terpeze or Smonice, after a trip that lasted some three or four hours, these two lads came and we continued the way towards Pagarushe through Malisheve. So we travelled by car along the main road because Malisheve is mostly inhabited by Albanians. And after the 1990s where it was -- its status was changed from municipality, it had no -- nothing, no state institution, no police station, no administrative building. So it was as easy for us to move around at night up to Pagarushe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Where were you aiming to go?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: Haxhi's cousin had found a provisional place for us to stay in Pagarushe, and we went there. We stayed there overnight, but it was a temporary stay. My purpose was to did to Klecke, because I felt safe there. It was my place of residence. I knew I could find a place to stay. Nobody could refuse us because it was normal for people to refuse you to stay with them at the time. They were afraid. But it was safe for me to go there. First I had to go to sound out the situation. We stayed in Pagarushe on one night. On the next day in the evening, we - Shukri and Agim - travelled to Klecke accompanied by these two lads, because at that time it was very dangerous for five people to stay together and even for people it was not easy to feed and to shelter five people. So Shukri and Agim together with Haxhi's cousin continued their trip to Klecke and went to Klecke at the house of my nephew who is a hero now. Sadik Shala is his name. I had told Sadik that he should tell my nephew that I had sent him. Shukri goes there and tells him that Fatmir had sent them and asked for his help. Sadik was a person who knew the terrain very well, so he helped them pass on to Lipjan and Stimlje municipalities. The three of us who remained went from Pagarushe to Goriq village. Goriq we -- we stayed with some acquaintances of Haxhi at the family of Zejnullah Mazreku. There we stayed for two days. I want to say here from the very first moment Zejnullah told us that his home was ours and that we could go there any time we needed and that he would take care of us. Or we could stay there because accommodation, shelter, was the number one necessity for us. After two days of stay in Goriq, we travelled in the direction of Klecke. In Goriq we had created a base that we might use -- make use of if the need arose. So after that we went to Klecke. All the time we travelled at night because we didn't know -- didn't want people to know about our movements. We arrived in Klecke in late evening, and Sadik came to meet us. And this is how it happened that we settled in Klecke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I have one more question tonight because it's now approaching 7.00, and that is this: Where are we in the -- are we still in March that you arrive in Klecka finally or have we got to April do you think?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ
utterances.text: No. I think it was the end of March. In might have been the 20th of March, probably. It was -- I know that it was the last part of March, the end of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mansfield. We will continue tomorrow afternoon at 2.15, and we will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 18th day of May, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
